analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to form unions and strengthens penalties on employers who violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The bill passed a Senate committee with 49 senators supporting it, but the full Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it easier for workers to join together in unions. It extends union protections to many workers currently classified as independent contractors, makes companies that share control over workers jointly responsible for obeying labor law, bans the permanent replacement of strikers, allows more coordinated strikes, speeds up union elections, and raises financial penalties for employers who fire or retaliate against workers who organize. It also overrides state 'right to work' laws that let workers in union shops avoid paying union fees. The bill was approved by the Senate committee that handles labor law in mid-2023 and placed on the Senate calendar, but it never received a vote by the full Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to unionize or who are currently misclassified as independent contractors, striking workers who would no longer face permanent replacement, and workers with union contracts through faster elections, joint-employer coverage, and much stiffer employer penalties. The biggest gains would go to workers in heavily union-hostile industries like warehouses, delivery, retail, hospitality, and gig platforms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, especially gig workers and strikers

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes the National Labor Relations Board's orders effective immediately and adds a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation for ignoring them, so employers can no longer delay compliance for years while appeals drag on.

Employers who fire or retaliate against organizing workers face civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat violations, and workers can sue directly for back pay, front pay, consequential damages, double liquidated damages, and punitive damages.

The bill makes it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace a worker who goes on strike, to lock out or suspend workers to influence bargaining, or to force workers to attend meetings aimed at discouraging union membership.

Under the bill's new employee test, workers are presumed to be employees rather than independent contractors unless they are free from the company's control, work outside its usual business, and have their own independent trade — a standard that would likely reclassify many gig workers.

Companies that share control over workers' wages, hours, and conditions are treated as joint employers, so franchisors and staffing platforms can no longer avoid bargaining and liability by pushing decisions down to franchisees and subcontractors.

The bill allows unions to honor other unions' picket lines through secondary strikes and prohibits employers from suing unions that do so, which gives workers in related workplaces real leverage to back each other up.

If an employer is found to have interfered with a representation election and a majority of workers signed union cards during the prior year, the bill lets the NLRB certify the union and order the employer to bargain instead of rerunning the election.

The bill overrides state right-to-work laws, letting collective bargaining agreements require every employee in the bargaining unit to contribute fees for the cost of representation, so workers can be required to share the cost of the union that represents them.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in union-active industries — large employers, franchise chains, staffing agencies, and gig platforms — bear the cost through higher penalties and direct lawsuits, joint-employer bargaining obligations with franchisees and subcontractors, faster elections, and binding first-contract arbitration where new unions get a two-year contract imposed by a panel if negotiations stall after mediation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers, franchisors, and gig platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state right-to-work laws and forces workers who choose not to join a union to still pay fees to it as a condition of employment, which many Americans see as coerced association.

The bill permits secondary strikes, where unions pressure a neutral employer to pressure their members' actual employer, which critics argue drags uninvolved businesses and their workers into other companies' disputes.

The bill imposes mandatory binding arbitration of first contracts after 90 days of bargaining plus 30 days of mediation, putting the terms of a two-year contract in the hands of a panel rather than the parties themselves.

Business groups argue faster elections with limited employer standing, immediate effect of board orders, and sharply increased penalties make union organizing procedurally one-sided and could raise labor costs that flow to consumers or reduce hiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want a union, the bill addresses real, well-documented problems: penalties today are small, elections are slow, and employers can litigate for years without complying. The costs are concentrated on employers and would partly flow through to consumers, and provisions like forced fee payment and secondary strikes genuinely burden people who oppose the union or are neutral bystanders. On balance it is a substantial pro-worker restructuring of labor law whose burden falls mainly on employers rather than on workers who don't want to organize.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill in July 2023 and put it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on February 28, 2023, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
On June 21, 2023, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on July 18, 2023, Senator Sanders reported it to the Senate without a written report.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 133 on July 18, 2023, and no further action was taken in the 118th Congress.

The bill had a Democratic cosponsor list of 47 Democrats plus Senator Sanders and Senator King, and Majority Leader Schumer was a cosponsor, but with the narrow 51-49 Senate it faced the same arithmetic that sank the 2021 House-passed version of the PRO Act, and no floor vote was ever scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and industries that oppose unionization — including large employers, franchise chains, and gig platforms — are better off because the bill died without a Senate vote; unions and union-seeking workers gained nothing beyond a committee approval that never led to law.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (I-VT) and committee chair, sponsor of the bill who reported it out of committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 28, 2023, and as chairman of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, reported it favorably to the Senate without amendment on July 18, 2023.

for.role: Majority members of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported without amendment favorably on June 21, 2023, sending it to the Senate floor.

for.name: Charles Schumer
for.role: Senate Majority Leader and cosponsor of the bill
for.what_they_did: Signed on as one of the original cosponsors but never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the 118th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican minority and Senate leadership
against.role: The 49 Republican senators and Senate floor managers
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and no floor vote was ever scheduled before the 118th Congress ended, so the bill died on the calendar.

against.name: United States Chamber of Commerce and business trade groups
against.role: National business associations representing employers, franchisors, and gig platforms
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the PRO Act as they had against the identical 2019-2021 version, opposing its joint-employer standard, secondary strikes, removal of state right-to-work rules, and expanded penalties.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 Senate cosponsors were Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats — 47 D and 1 I — with no Republican support, and no floor vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill's new employee test would likely force platforms to reclassify many drivers and couriers as employees entitled to unionize, raising labor costs sharply. Workers on those platforms would gain organizing rights but some could lose the scheduling flexibility the contractor model offers.

The joint-employer definition makes franchisors and parent companies bargaining partners and liability targets for their franchisees' labor practices, forcing companies like McDonald's to bargain directly over restaurant-level wages and conditions rather than pushing those decisions to franchisees.

Companies like Amazon, Starbucks, Tesla, and Walmart face faster elections, immediate enforcement of NLRB orders, up to $50,000 in penalties per violation plus double liquidated damages and direct lawsuits for firing or retaliating against organizers, and mandatory first-contract arbitration. Workers who organize there gain substantial new legal tools.
Joint-employer liability extends organizing rights and labor costs across staffing and contractor arrangements that firms currently use to keep unions out of the worksite.

The bill gives unions faster elections, secondary-strike leverage, automatic fee collection over state right-to-work laws, and employer penalties that make retaliation costly, all of which strengthen unions' ability to organize and win contracts.
